0.title: Obadiah: The Kingdom Shall Be the LORD's
0.overview:
The message. Obadiah is God’s answer to a question every wounded believer asks: did God see what was done to us, and will he do anything about it? When Jerusalem fell, Edom, Israel’s brother nation, stood by, gloated, looted and handed over the refugees. Obadiah announces that God saw it all: “The pride of your heart has deceived you” (v. 3), and “As you have done, it shall be done to you” (v. 15). Every power that thinks no one can touch it will fall, but God will keep a rescued people on Mount Zion. The book’s last words are the last word of history: “the kingdom shall be the LORD’s” (v. 21).

Background: the writer. The shortest book in the Old Testament, twenty-one verses, tells us nothing about its writer but his name, which means “servant of the LORD”. Jewish tradition identified him with the Obadiah who hid the LORD’s prophets in Ahab’s day (1 Kings 18:3–4), but nothing in the book supports this. He gives no king, no father and no home town, only “The vision of Obadiah” (v. 1).

Edom: a brother turned enemy. Edom lay south-east of the Dead Sea, a high land of red sandstone cliffs and narrow gorges; the later rock city of Petra lies in the same hills. Its people descended from Esau, the twin brother of Jacob. Before the twins were born the LORD told Rebekah, “Two nations are in your womb” (Genesis 25:23). The brothers were reconciled (Genesis 33:4), but their descendants never were, though God’s law said, “You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother” (Deuteronomy 23:7). Centuries of border wars followed. Amos condemned Edom “because he pursued his brother with the sword and cast off all pity” (Amos 1:11).

When? Obadiah names no king, so Christians differ over his date. Most place him soon after Nebuchadnezzar’s army destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC, since verses 11–14 read like a fresh memory of that day, and other Scriptures accuse Edom of exactly this: “Remember, O LORD, against the Edomites the day of Jerusalem” (Psalm 137:7). Others place him about 845 BC, when Edom rebelled against Judah (2 Kings 8:20–22) and raiders plundered Jerusalem and the king’s house (2 Chronicles 21:16–17). Much of Obadiah runs parallel to Jeremiah’s oracle on Edom (Jeremiah 49:7–22), and scholars debate which came first. This commentary does not press a date, though the later setting explains verses 11–14 most naturally. Nothing in the message depends on the year.

The kind of writing. Obadiah is a prophetic oracle against a foreign nation, in Hebrew poetry, like those in Isaiah 13–23 and Jeremiah 46–51. Such oracles were spoken less to the nations named than to God’s own people: Edom probably never heard this book, but Judah did, among the ruins. It speaks of the future as already done, because God has said it, and it sees one nation’s reckoning as a preview of “the day of the LORD” on all the nations (v. 15).

How the book makes its case. First comes the verdict (verses 1–9): God summons the nations against Edom and strips away everything it trusted, one layer at a time: its fortress “in the clefts of the rock” (v. 3), its hidden treasure, its allies, its wise men and its soldiers. Then comes the charge (verses 10–14): “the violence done to your brother Jacob” (v. 10). Edom “stood aloof” while strangers looted Jerusalem, and God’s verdict on the bystander is “you were like one of them” (v. 11). Eight commands trace a terrible progression, from gloating and boasting to looting and at last catching the fugitives at the crossroads to hand them over. What began with a look ended in murder. Last comes the horizon (verses 15–21): the day of the LORD on every nation, with exact repayment as its rule. But judgment is not the last word: “But in Mount Zion there shall be those who escape, and it shall be holy” (v. 17). The scattered exiles come home to more than they lost, and “Saviors shall go up to Mount Zion to rule Mount Esau, and the kingdom shall be the LORD’s” (v. 21).

A hard word against a nation? Verse 18, with “no survivor for the house of Esau”, is hard to read. But the book is not a curse spoken in revenge. It is God’s sentence on a people who showed no mercy, and it leaves the reckoning with God, as the New Testament does: “Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19). History bore it out: within a few generations Edom’s kingdom had collapsed, Arab peoples such as the Nabataeans took its hills, and its people, pushed west into southern Judah (later called Idumea), vanish from history after the first century AD. Yet the door was never shut to Edomites themselves: Amos heard God promise that the restored house of David would possess “the remnant of Edom” (Amos 9:12). This commentary’s view is that the nation which fought God’s people perished, while sinners from every nation, Israel’s old enemies included, are welcomed in Christ.

Where Christians differ. How is the promise of land in verses 19–20 fulfilled? Dispensationalists look for a literal future possession by the nation of Israel. This commentary reads it, with the New Testament, as fulfilled in part in the return from exile and fully in Christ’s kingdom, whose meek “shall inherit the earth” (Matthew 5:5).

Where it leads: to Christ. Obadiah leads to Christ by the need it exposes, by contrast and by promise. The need: if the rule of the last day is “As you have done, it shall be done to you” (v. 15), none of us could stand. The cup of judgment in verse 16 is the cup Jesus faced in Gethsemane: “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39). At the cross he received what we had done, so that we might receive what he deserved. The contrast: Edom stood aloof from its brother on the day of his ruin, but Christ came down into ours, and “he is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11). The promise: the rescued people on Mount Zion are those who trust him, for “you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God” and “to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant” (Hebrews 12:22, 24). When James quoted Amos at the council in Jerusalem, he followed the Greek Old Testament, which read “Edom” as “mankind”: “that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by my name” (Acts 15:17). Edom’s remnant had widened into the world. Later still, Herod the Great, a king of Edomite descent, tried to kill the infant Jesus (Matthew 2:16), and failed. The end Obadiah saw will be announced in heaven: “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ” (Revelation 11:15).

For us. To anyone who has been wronged and wondered whether God noticed, Obadiah says that he saw every detail and that the reckoning may be left to him. To anyone tempted to stand aloof, or to enjoy the fall of someone they resent, it says that God counts the bystander among the attackers, and that gloating is where cruelty begins. The gospel cuts the root of it, because at the cross we learn that we are not spectators at someone else’s judgment: we deserved it, and Christ took our place. And they need not fear the powers that look unshakeable, for “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6), and the kingdom shall be the LORD’s.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Pride of Your Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God summons the nations against Edom (vv. 1-2). Proud in its rock fortresses, Edom will be brought down (vv. 3-4), stripped bare and betrayed by its allies (vv. 5-7), its wisdom and its soldiers failing (vv. 8-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Pride deceives, and no height, wealth or cleverness can keep anyone safe from God.

verseByVerse.quote: The vision of Obadiah. Thus says the Lord GOD concerning Edom: We have heard a report from the LORD, and a messenger has been sent among the nations: "Rise up! Let us rise against her for battle!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The vision of Obadiah. We know nothing about Obadiah except his name: no king, no date, no family. What we have is a vision from God concerning Edom.

The date. Most date the book soon after 586 BC, when the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem, because verses 11-14 describe foreigners casting lots for the city while Edom looked on. Psalm 137 remembers that day and prays, Remember, O LORD, against the Edomites the day of Jerusalem (Ps 137:7). Others believe he preached much earlier, in the ninth century BC (about 845 BC), when Edom rebelled against Judah (2 Kgs 8:20-22) and raiders plundered Jerusalem and the royal household (2 Chr 21:16-17). Nothing in the message depends on settling it. Either way, the first hearers were people of Judah who had watched a brother nation turn on them in their worst hour, and the vision was given to assure them that God had seen it all and that the last word was his (v. 21).

Obadiah and Jeremiah. Much of Obadiah is very like Jeremiah 49:7-22. Some think Jeremiah drew on Obadiah, some the reverse, and others that both used an older oracle about Edom; the message is the same either way.

A messenger has been sent among the nations. The prophet has overheard heaven's news: a messenger is stirring up the nations for war against Edom. Nations imagine they choose their own wars. Obadiah shows that God is the one who actually moves them.
verseByVerse.note: The name Obadiah means "servant of the LORD"; about a dozen different men in the Old Testament bear it.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I will make you small among the nations; you shall be utterly despised. The pride of your heart has deceived you, you who live in the clefts of the rock, in your lofty dwelling, who say in your heart, "Who will bring me down to the ground?" Though you soar aloft like the eagle, though your nest is set among the stars, from there I will bring you down, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will make you small among the nations. Edom's future is settled in one sentence. (The ESV notes that it may be read as already accomplished: "Behold, I have made you small".)

Who were the Edomites? They were the descendants of Esau, Jacob's twin brother (Gen 36:1). The feud began before the twins were born, when God said, Two nations are in your womb (Gen 25:23). Esau sold his birthright, lost the blessing, and hated Jacob (Gen 27:41). The brothers were later reconciled, and Esau ran to meet Jacob, embraced him and fell on his neck and kissed him (Gen 33:4). But their descendants kept the quarrel alive for a thousand years. Edom refused Israel passage on the way to the promised land (Num 20:18), even though God's law said, You shall not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother (Deut 23:7).

Was Edom doomed from birth? Readers who know Malachi's words, I have loved Jacob but Esau I have hated (Mal 1:2-3), which Paul uses of God's free choice in grace (Rom 9:13), may wonder whether Edom was simply doomed from birth. Obadiah does not argue that way. He names what Edom did, its pride and its cruelty to a brother, and judges it for that. God's free choice and real human guilt stand side by side in Scripture, and neither cancels the other.

The pride of your heart has deceived you. Pride is a liar. It tells us we are safe, self-sufficient and beyond correction, and by the time we discover otherwise it is too late.

You who live in the clefts of the rock. Edom’s pride rested on where it lived. The people lived in the clefts of the rock (the ESV notes this may be a place name, "Sela", meaning a rock stronghold), in the high red sandstone country southeast of the Dead Sea, on cliffs reached through narrow gorges; the rock city of Petra, carved by a later people, lies in that region. It is one thing to feel secure; it is another to say in your heart that nobody, not even God, can touch you.

Though you soar aloft like the eagle. However high Edom sets its nest, like the eagle, God reaches higher. The same charge was laid against Babylon, whose king said, I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will set my throne on high (Isa 14:13). Height is no defence when God is the one who brings you down.

Our own fortresses. Every reader needs this. Our fortresses are usually not cliffs but savings, qualifications, reputation, health or family. None of them are wrong in themselves, and all of them can quietly make us feel that no one could ever bring us down. God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble (Jas 4:6). Jesus said, everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 18:14). It is far better to come down willingly now, into the arms of the God who gives grace to the humble, than to be brought down at the last.
verseByVerse.note: Sela is probably the rock stronghold that King Amaziah of Judah captured and renamed Joktheel (2 Kgs 14:7).

verseByVerse.quote: If thieves came to you, if plunderers came by night— how you have been destroyed!— would they not steal only enough for themselves? If grape gatherers came to you, would they not leave gleanings? How Esau has been pillaged, his treasures sought out! All your allies have driven you to your border; those at peace with you have deceived you; they have prevailed against you; those who eat your bread have set a trap beneath you— you have no understanding.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If thieves came to you. Obadiah uses two pictures from ordinary life. Thieves take what they can carry and leave the rest; grape pickers always miss a few bunches, and the poor came behind to gather them. Even a robbery and a harvest leave something behind. But when God deals with Edom, nothing will be left. Their hidden treasures, stored in caves and cliff strongholds, will be sought out. The prophet breaks into the middle of his own sentence with a cry: how you have been destroyed! He speaks as if it has already happened, because God has said it.

Those at peace with you have deceived you. Edom sat on important trade routes and knew how to make friends with the strong. Now those friends, the ones at the dinner table, set the trap. (The ESV notes that the Hebrew of this line is compressed, so that the words those who eat are supplied, and that it reads "he has set a trap".) Edom, who betrayed a brother, is betrayed by friends. In time Edom was indeed driven out of its ancient territory, probably by Arab peoples such as the Nabataeans in the centuries after the exile, and had to settle further west in southern Judah, which came to be called Idumea.

You have no understanding. Edom was famous for its clever men, and it had no understanding of this. Worldly cleverness can solve many problems, but it has no answer when God acts.

verseByVerse.quote: Will I not on that day, declares the LORD, destroy the wise men out of Edom, and understanding out of Mount Esau? And your mighty men shall be dismayed, O Teman, so that every man from Mount Esau will be cut off by slaughter.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Destroy the wise men out of Edom. Edom had a reputation for wisdom. Jeremiah asks, Is wisdom no more in Teman? (Jer 49:7), and Job's friend Eliphaz was a Temanite, from Edomite territory (Job 2:11). Wisdom is God's gift, and he can withdraw it. A nation can lose the ability to think clearly about its own danger.

Your mighty men shall be dismayed. The mighty men will be dismayed, their courage gone before the battle. One layer at a time God takes away the cliffs (vv. 3-4), the hidden treasure (vv. 5-6), the allies (v. 7), the wise men (v. 8), and now the soldiers. It is a sober picture of what happens when God finally deals with human pride: not a fair fight, but a quiet collapse.
verseByVerse.note: Teman, named after a grandson of Esau (Gen 36:11), often stands for Edom as a whole.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–14 — The Day of Your Brother
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The charge is violence against your brother Jacob: on the day Jerusalem fell, Edom stood aloof and was like one of them (vv. 10-11). Eight commands name what Edom did, from gloating to cutting off the fugitives (vv. 12-14).
verseByVerse.theology: Standing by while others suffer, and gloating over a brother's ruin, are sins God takes personally.

verseByVerse.quote: Because of the violence done to your brother Jacob, shame shall cover you, and you shall be cut off forever. On the day that you stood aloof, on the day that strangers carried off his wealth and foreigners entered his gates and cast lots for Jerusalem, you were like one of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your brother Jacob. The key word in the charge is brother. God had protected Edom's land when Israel marched to Canaan and forbidden Israel to despise them. Edom's violence was against family.

When it is family. God notices what families and churches do to their own. The closer the tie, the deeper the wound, and the more seriously he takes it.

On the day that you stood aloof. Here is the scene: Jerusalem has fallen. Foreign soldiers pour through the broken gates, carry off everything of value and gamble for the city as if it were a prize. And where was Edom? You stood aloof. In verse 11 they do not even swing a sword. They simply stood and watched their brother being destroyed.

You were like one of them. In God's eyes the bystander had joined the attackers. Standing aside is a choice. It was the sin of the priest and the Levite who crossed the road and left the wounded man (Luke 10:31-32), and it is the sin John describes when he asks how God's love can be in a person who sees his brother in need, yet closes his heart against him (1 John 3:17). Whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin (Jas 4:17).

verseByVerse.quote: But do not gloat over the day of your brother in the day of his misfortune; do not rejoice over the people of Judah in the day of their ruin; do not boast in the day of distress. Do not enter the gate of my people in the day of their calamity; do not gloat over his disaster in the day of his calamity; do not loot his wealth in the day of his calamity. Do not stand at the crossroads to cut off his fugitives; do not hand over his survivors in the day of distress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The day of your brother. The word day beats through these eight commands like a drum. God is not giving Edom advice for next time; each command describes a crime Edom had already committed.

How sin grows. Watch the progression, because it is the way sin always grows. It begins in the eyes: do not gloat. Then it reaches the heart: do not rejoice. Then it comes out of the mouth: do not boast (the ESV notes the Hebrew is vivid, "do not enlarge your mouth"). Then the feet move: Do not enter the gate of my people. Then the hands take: do not loot his wealth. Finally the worst of all: standing at the crossroads to catch the refugees running for their lives, and handing the survivors over to the enemy. What began as a look ended in murder.

The gate of my people. In the middle of this God calls Judah my people. Even in the hour when he was judging them, they were still his, and he was watching how others treated them.

The sin of quiet gloating. This is the searching part of Obadiah for ordinary readers. Few of us will ever plunder a city. But the quiet pleasure at the downfall of someone we resent (the colleague who failed, the church that split, the family member whose marriage collapsed) is the very sin God names first. Scripture says plainly, Do not rejoice when your enemy falls, and let not your heart be glad when he stumbles (Prov 24:17). The gloating heart is only the beginning, but it is a real beginning. When we find that pleasure in ourselves, the answer is not to despair but to confess it to the Christ who prayed for those who mocked him (Luke 23:34), and whose Spirit teaches us to weep with those who weep (Rom 12:15).

The pleasure of watching someone fall. German has a word for it, Schadenfreude, and our culture has built an industry on it. Whole channels of news and entertainment live on the downfall of the famous, and a stranger’s worst moment can be watched, shared and mocked by millions before nightfall. Why does it feel so good? Because another person’s fall quietly tells me that I am better than him. Gloating is a way of justifying ourselves on the cheap: I have not done much, but at least I am not her. That is why religious people are as prone to it as anyone; it is the moralist’s favourite pleasure, and the cynic’s too. Edom stood by and enjoyed it, and the enjoyment was the beginning of murder. The gospel cuts the root, because it tells us we have no standing of our own to protect. We are not spectators at someone else’s judgment; we were the ones who deserved it, and Christ came down from the heights and took our place in the ruins. People who know that cannot easily enjoy a fall. They are too busy being grateful that they were caught.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–21 — The Kingdom Shall Be the LORD's
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The day of the LORD comes on all nations, and each will be repaid (vv. 15-16). But Zion will have survivors and be holy (vv. 17-18), God's people will possess the land (vv. 19-20), and the kingdom shall be the LORD's (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: History ends not with Edom or any empire, but with salvation on Mount Zion and the kingdom of God.

verseByVerse.quote: For the day of the LORD is near upon all the nations. As you have done, it shall be done to you; your deeds shall return on your own head. For as you have drunk on my holy mountain, so all the nations shall drink continually; they shall drink and swallow, and shall be as though they had never been.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Near upon all the nations. The message suddenly widens from one small nation to all the nations. Edom is one example. What God does to Edom, he will do to every proud and cruel power, because he is the God of the whole earth.

As you have done, it shall be done to you. The rule of that day is simple. Edom cut off fugitives, and Edom will be cut off (v. 9). Edom looted, and Edom will be pillaged (v. 6). Jesus stated the same principle: with the measure you use it will be measured to you (Matt 7:2), and Paul warned, whatever one sows, that will he also reap (Gal 6:7).

Our own case. None of us would survive a judgment that gave us back exactly what we have given others.

As you have drunk on my holy mountain. The word drunk may look back to Edom celebrating on my holy mountain, God's temple hill, while Jerusalem burned; it is a picture of revelling in another's ruin. It may also point forward to the cup of God's wrath that the prophets often describe: in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine (Ps 75:8), which God made the nations drink (Jer 25:15-17). Most likely both are in view: they drank in triumph, and now they will drink judgment. The end is total: they will be as though they had never been.

The cup Christ drank. The only way to escape that cup is that Someone else drank it. At the cross, Christ received the punishment for what we had done, so that we might receive what he deserved. In Gethsemane Jesus prayed, My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will (Matt 26:39), and then said, shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me? (John 18:11). He drank it to the dregs for his people.

verseByVerse.quote: But in Mount Zion there shall be those who escape, and it shall be holy, and the house of Jacob shall possess their own possessions. The house of Jacob shall be a fire, and the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau stubble; they shall burn them and consume them, and there shall be no survivor for the house of Esau, for the LORD has spoken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Mount Zion there shall be those who escape. Judgment is not the last word. Verse 17 begins with But, one of the great words of the Bible. On the hill where Edom had celebrated, God will keep a rescued people. Joel had said the same: in Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there shall be those who escape (Joel 2:32), and he added the promise that everyone who calls on the name of the LORD shall be saved.

It shall be holy. Zion shall be holy, cleansed of everything that defiled it, and God's people will get back what was taken from them. Believers have already come to that Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, and to Jesus, the mediator of a new covenant (Heb 12:22, 24).

The house of Esau stubble. Edom had seemed as permanent as its cliffs; before God's people it will prove as flimsy as dry stubble before a flame. The house of Jacob and the house of Joseph are the southern and northern tribes together, reunited in God's purpose.

Facing hard words. These are hard words, and honesty requires us to feel their weight. They are God's sentence on a nation that had shown no mercy, and Edom did eventually disappear as a people. Yet even here the door is not shut against individual Edomites: the restored kingdom of David would include the remnant of Edom (Amos 9:12; Acts 15:16-17). The nation that fought God's people perished; sinners from every nation, including Israel's old enemies, are welcomed in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Those of the Negeb shall possess Mount Esau, and those of the Shephelah shall possess the land of the Philistines; they shall possess the land of Ephraim and the land of Samaria, and Benjamin shall possess Gilead. The exiles of this host of the people of Israel shall possess the land of the Canaanites as far as Zarephath, and the exiles of Jerusalem who are in Sepharad shall possess the cities of the Negeb. Saviors shall go up to Mount Zion to rule Mount Esau, and the kingdom shall be the LORD's.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those of the Negeb shall possess Mount Esau. The verses sweep around the compass. The Negeb is the dry south, the Shephelah the low hills west toward Philistia, Ephraim and Samaria the central highlands, and Gilead the land east of the Jordan. Zarephath lay up the coast in Phoenicia, where Elijah once stayed with a widow (1 Kgs 17:9). Sepharad is a place we cannot identify with certainty; it has often been connected with Sardis in Asia Minor, and Jewish readers in the Middle Ages took it to mean Spain, which is why Jews of Spanish descent are still called Sephardic. The point of the list is not geography but reversal: the people who lost everything will be given more than they lost, and the scattered exiles will come home.

Saviors shall go up to Mount Zion. Saviors is the word used for the deliverers God raised up in the days of the judges (Judg 3:9; Neh 9:27): men who rescued his people when they cried to him. From Zion they rule Mount Esau, the proud height that thought itself untouchable.

The kingdom shall be the LORD’s. The book ends in one magnificent line, the kingdom shall be the LORD’s, which is the point of the whole book. The kingdom belongs not to Edom, Babylon or any power that seems to own the future, but to God, and one day everyone will see it. Zechariah says it too: the LORD will be king over all the earth (Zech 14:9).

How it comes about. The New Testament shows us how it comes about. There is one Savior who went up to Mount Zion, and he is the Lord himself. Jesus Christ was crucified outside Jerusalem, rose, and ascended to reign, and at the end the announcement rings out, The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever (Rev 11:15). Centuries after Obadiah, Herod the Great, a king of Edomite descent, tried to kill the infant Jesus (Matt 2:16). Esau's line made one last attempt on the child of Jacob's line, and failed. Within about a century the Idumeans, as Edom's descendants were then called, had vanished from history; the King they tried to kill reigns forever.

Three things to keep. So this little book leaves the believer, who has been shown mercy, with three things. Do not be proud, because God brings the high down. Do not gloat over anyone's fall, because God is watching how we treat our brothers. And do not fear the Edoms of this world, however secure they look: the kingdom shall be the LORD's.

How is the possession of these lands fulfilled? Partly in the return after the exile; fully in Christ’s kingdom, where his people inherit the earth (Matt 5:5). Dispensationalists look for a literal future possession by Israel, because they read the land promises as still awaiting fulfilment for the nation; this commentary reads them, with the New Testament, as widened in Christ to the whole earth (Rom 4:13), and gladly acknowledges that faithful Christians differ here. The “saviors” of verse 21 are deliverers God raises up, fulfilled in Christ and in his people who share his reign (Rev 3:21); the kingdom shall be the LORD’s has begun in Christ and will be complete when he returns.

1.title: The Kingdom Shall Be the LORD's
1.overview:
Obadiah's one chapter moves in three steps. First God announces that proud Edom, safe in its cliffs, will be brought down (vv. 1-9). Then he names the reason: when Jerusalem fell, Edom stood by, gloated and joined in against its own brother (vv. 10-14).

Finally the view widens to the day of the LORD on all nations, and the book ends not with Edom's ruin but with rescue on Mount Zion and the promise that the kingdom shall be the LORD's (vv. 15-21).
1.theology:
God rules the nations and moves them as he wills, even when they think they are choosing their own wars (v. 1).

Pride deceives; no fortress, wealth or cleverness can protect anyone from God, who opposes the proud (vv. 3-4, 8-9; Isa 14:13-14; Jas 4:6; Luke 18:14).

God takes wrongs done within the family of his people personally, and counts the bystander among the attackers (vv. 10-11; Luke 10:31-32; 1 John 3:17; Jas 4:17).

Gloating over another's downfall is sin, and it is where cruelty begins (vv. 12-14; Prov 24:17-18).

God repays what people have done, and Christ drank the cup of that judgment in his people's place (vv. 15-16; Matt 7:2; Gal 6:7; Ps 75:8; Matt 26:39; John 18:11).

God preserves a people who escape, and makes Zion holy; believers have come to the heavenly Zion in Christ (v. 17; Joel 2:32; Heb 12:22-24).

Judgment on hostile nations and mercy to individuals from them belong together: a remnant of Edom is promised to the kingdom of David's Son (v. 18; Amos 9:12; Acts 15:16-17).

History ends with salvation on Mount Zion and with God's kingdom, established by Jesus Christ, the true Savior and King (v. 21; Judg 3:9; Zech 14:9; Rev 11:15).
1.examples:
Edom nested in its cliffs and asked who could ever bring it down. God answered by taking away, one by one, everything it trusted, until even the friends at its table set a trap for it. Our own fortresses are more often savings, reputation or health than rock, and they can be held humbly or proudly.

Edom's sin began with a brother standing at a distance, watching a city burn; the look became a cheer, the cheer a robbery, and the robbery ended with refugees caught at the crossroads. The quiet pleasure we take in someone's fall is the same sin at its beginning, and it can be confessed to the Christ who prayed for those who mocked him.

The cup Edom passed round in triumph became the cup of judgment, and Christ drank that cup for his people. So the book ends not with stubble where a fortress stood but with saviors on Zion and a kingdom that belongs to God alone.
